tasks.gr12-mid-latitude-cyclones-t1: Topic: Mid-latitude cyclones. Cover the polar front, warm sector, cold front, occluded front, westerlies, the life cycle of a mid-latitude cyclone, and the weather changes that affect South Africa as fronts pass. Ask Grade 12 learners to interpret synoptic charts, explain rainfall patterns, or compare front-related weather conditions.
tasks.gr12-tropical-cyclones-anticyclones-t1: Topic: Tropical cyclones and anticyclones. Cover the conditions needed for tropical cyclone formation, the eye and eyewall, hazards such as storm surge and flooding, and the subsiding dry air found in anticyclones over southern Africa. Ask Grade 12 learners to compare pressure systems or explain tropical storm impacts.
tasks.gr12-local-climates-t1: Topic: Local climates. Cover valley climates, slope aspect, mountain and valley breezes, temperature inversions, frost pockets, urban heat islands, pollution domes, and how land use changes local weather. Ask Grade 12 learners to explain microclimate differences or interpret settlement choices.
tasks.gr12-fluvial-processes-catchment-managem: Topic: Fluvial processes and catchment management. Cover drainage basins, watersheds, tributaries, stream order, river erosion, transport and deposition, drainage patterns, and catchment management in South Africa. Ask Grade 12 learners to interpret river diagrams or explain flood-control strategies.
tasks.gr12-map-scale-distance-area-t1: Topic: Map Scale, Distance and Area (Grade 12 mapwork). Cover word, ratio and line scales (1:50 000 means 1 cm on the map is 500 m on the ground), converting map distance to ground distance and back, measuring straight and curved routes (sum of straight pieces), finding the scale from a map distance and a ground distance, large and small scales (1:10 000 is larger than 1:50 000), and area: convert both map lengths to ground lengths then multiply; the 2 cm grid squares of a 1:50 000 map are 1 km by 1 km = 1 km2; 1 km2 = 100 ha. Describe each map in numbers in the question (there is no picture); never invent place names or use real map sheets. Write units always (m, km, km2, ha) with a decimal comma. Ask Grade 12 learners to calculate.
tasks.gr12-bearings-declination-t1: Topic: Direction, Bearings and Magnetic Declination (Grade 12 mapwork). Cover the 16 compass points and their true bearings (N 000, E 090, S 180, W 270; NE 045, SE 135, SW 225, NW 315), bearings measured clockwise from north and written with three digits, the back bearing (add or subtract 180), the bearing from east and north offsets, and magnetic declination: in South Africa magnetic north lies WEST of true north, so magnetic bearing = true bearing + declination and true = magnetic - declination; the declination for the present year from the map's base year and mean annual change in minutes (for example 24 degrees 10 minutes W in 2006 increasing 6 minutes a year gives 26 degrees 10 minutes W in 2026), carrying 60 minutes into 1 degree. Give the declination in the question; never assume a value. Describe each situation in numbers (there is no picture). Ask Grade 12 learners to calculate.
tasks.gr12-contours-gradient-sections-t1: Topic: Contours, Gradient, Cross-sections and Intervisibility (Grade 12 mapwork). Cover contour lines and the contour interval (close lines = steep, far apart = gentle; rings rising inwards = hill; contours cross a river in a V that points upstream), gradient = vertical interval / horizontal distance written 1:x (smaller x = steeper; convert the map distance to metres first), cross-sections (plot heights above a base line; 1 cm = 20 m style vertical scale), vertical exaggeration = horizontal scale / vertical scale (1:50 000 and 1 cm = 20 m gives 25 times), and intervisibility (two points can see each other only if every point between them is below the straight line of sight). Describe each map or section in numbers and heights (there is no picture); never invent place names. Write units and a decimal comma. Ask Grade 12 learners to calculate and reason.
tasks.gr12-aerial-orthophoto-t1: Topic: Aerial Photographs and Orthophoto Maps (Grade 12 mapwork). Cover vertical aerial photographs (camera straight down, plan view, used for mapping and measuring) and oblique photographs (tilted, horizon visible, scale changes), reading a vertical photograph by tone (dark: deep water, tar, dense trees; light: dry bare ground, sand, roofs), texture (smooth: grass and ploughed fields; rough: forest and rocks), shadow (height and shape) and pattern (straight lines and blocks made by people), orthophoto maps (corrected aerial photographs with the same scale all over, made at 1:10 000 for use with 1:50 000 maps, so 1 km is 10 cm), comparing an orthophoto map with a topographic map (real appearance versus symbols and names), finding the scale of a photograph from a photo distance and a ground distance, and orienting a photograph by matching features. Describe each photograph in words (there is no picture). Ask Grade 12 learners to identify, compare and calculate.
